questions.explanation: The rule is asserting a path, not a defect. It has found that a value which can be shaped by whoever sends the input can reach a place where a particular kind of action is performed, and it is claiming that on some path the value arrives there unaltered in the sense that matters, so the action is performed on attacker-chosen content. That is a real and useful claim, because the two things a review has to establish by hand are exactly these: where the value comes from, and where it goes, and both are spread across code that nobody reads end to end. The important qualifier is that the rule's conclusion is conditional on the path it found being the path that is taken. Code has branches, and a path that a particular route through the program does not exercise is a path that may not exist for the value in question, which is why a firing rule is a question about the code rather than a statement about what an attacker can actually do. That is also why a good rule set is a set of questions and a good reviewer treats the output as a work list ordered by how much of the path they believe. The first distractor describes a rule that has already done that work, and such a rule is either very narrow or unsound. The second confuses the direction of the claim: the rule does not say the sink is reachable by the attacker, only that the sink is reachable by the data. The third treats the absence of a firing as evidence, which is a claim about coverage rather than about safety.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rule has established that the path is ever taken.

questions.explanation: The reason is almost always that the rule has no way to represent the fact that the value is made safe on the way, so it reports the sanitised case identically to the unsanitised one. A rule that tracks where a value came from and where it went has no model of the program's intent, and a function that rewrites a value into a safe form, a comparison against a fixed set, or a call into a validator is invisible to it unless the rule has been told about that specific function by hand. So the precision of the rule set is a property of the configuration rather than of the analyser, and a rule that is wrong often enough teaches the team that its output means nothing, which is the correct lesson and the wrong remedy. The cost of turning it off is that the one class of defect the tool was good at finding stops being found by anything, and it is worth noticing that this is a real loss rather than a neutral one: a rule that is silent about a category is indistinguishable from a program with no flaw of that category, which is the confusion the whole practice of recording what a tool was not looking for exists to prevent. The productive response is to tune the rule set against what the codebase actually does, to accept that some findings will be false and sort them in a way that keeps the true ones visible, and to keep the tool running with a high volume rather than switching it off and losing the category. The first distractor blames the analyser rather than its configuration. The second is the right instinct applied to the wrong mechanism. The third claims turning it off is a net gain, which is true only of the review time and not of the coverage.

questions.explanation: The gap is the difference between what the code says and what the code does, and it is a large gap because code is full of paths that are only taken for particular inputs, particular states, and particular orderings that nobody wrote down. A dynamic test resolves all of that for the case it actually exercised: it knows which code ran, what the values were at the point they mattered, what came back, and how long each step took, and it knows this about the run rather than about the source. That is the reason a dynamic test finds things a reader does not: configuration read from the environment, defaults that differ from the documented ones, a library behaving differently than its interface suggests, a branch that only fires for a particular sequence, and a timing property that is simply not visible in the code at all. The cost is the mirror image, and it is not a small cost. A dynamic test only knows about the cases it ran, so a defect that requires an input the generator never produced is invisible to it, and the proportion of the program a single run covers is usually small. So the two approaches fail in opposite directions, one over-reporting and one under-reporting, and neither gives coverage of the space between. The first distractor describes a static property. questions.explanation: Without a measure of progress the whole approach collapses, because random mutation on a program with a large input space almost never produces the structured value that a particular branch needs. A parser wants a thousand records in a particular order; a length check wants a field of a particular size; a state machine wants a particular sequence of transitions. Each of those is a needle, and a fuzzer that cannot tell whether it is getting closer will not find it, which is why the naive version of the technique is largely ineffective on real parsers and protocol handlers. The measure changes the search from a walk through the whole space into a hill climb. The fuzzer records which parts of the program a run reached, keeps the input that reached a new part, and uses that as the starting point for the next round of mutations, so each generation is a variation on something that worked rather than a fresh throw. This is why the technique is effective on code that handles structure, and it also explains its characteristic failure: a defect that is reachable without any of those preconditions is found almost immediately by the random part, while a defect that requires an exact multi-step state is found only if the intermediate states are all individually reachable and individually recorded. The first distractor claims the measure is a speed optimisation. The second mistakes the corpus for the goal rather than the means. The third describes the behaviour of a fuzzer that has lost its corpus, which reverts it to random search.

questions.explanation: The consequence is that the fuzzer has no memory of anything that worked and is confined to the neighbourhood of the one input it was given. That neighbourhood is often much smaller than it sounds: if the target validates a header and rejects anything else, most mutations are rejected before the interesting code is reached at all, and a fuzzer that discards rejected runs has learned nothing from them beyond that they failed. So the campaign's reach is a function of how much structure one example happens to expose, and the tool will report a low rate of findings that says more about the example than about the target. This is a common and expensive configuration mistake, because the campaign looks like it is running and the dashboard looks like it is progressing, and the failure is only visible as an absence. questions.explanation: The version string is a claim made by the thing being scanned, about itself, and it is the first thing to be wrong. Vendors distribute fixes out of band, backport them into older versions without changing the version number, repackage, and redistribute, so a host reporting 2.4 may have every fix that 2.5 has and a host reporting 2.5 may not have a fix that was issued for a different build line. The version also does not identify the build, since the same version number is used across operating systems, architectures, and repackaging, and the part that was actually patched is often a shared library whose version the banner does not mention at all. So the mapping from a reported version to a patch level is a table somebody maintains by hand, it is maintained for the most common configurations, and it is wrong for everything else, and it rots. The finding is therefore evidence that a host claims to be running something in a range, which is a starting point for a conversation and not a conclusion about the host. The check that settles it is to ask the host what it actually has, which for a well-behaved program means asking for its installed patch inventory rather than its banner, and where that is not available the honest thing is to record the uncertainty in the finding. questions.explanation: A severity score is a statement about the weakness, computed from properties of the weakness itself: what kind of damage it does, whether it needs a user's action, how much privilege it needs to start from, and whether its scope crosses a boundary. Reachability is not in that list, and it cannot be, because the same weakness on two hosts in different positions has genuinely different consequences and a single number cannot express both. The judgement that has to be made separately is a set of positional facts: can anything outside reach the service, what has to happen before the weakness can be used, whether a compensating control sits in front of it, and what an attacker already on the segment would have. Those facts turn a weakness into an exposure, and they are the part a team can actually do something about, because they are what decides where the limited time of a remediation team goes. A useful form of the judgement separates the weakness from the work: what the weakness would let someone do, and what it would take to reach it here. The first distractor treats the score as already containing reachability, which is the confusion the separate step exists to prevent. The second assumes isolation is a property of the weakness rather than of the deployment. questions.explanation: The analysis tracks values as they move through code, and the representation of a value changes at the boundary. A buffer in one language and a string object in another are different kinds of thing to the two analysers, and the rules that know how to follow a buffer in the first one have no rule for the second, so the flow simply stops being tracked at the point where the type changes. There are further problems in the same place: the code that does the dangerous thing may be in a component with no source available at all, and the connection between the two may be a message on a queue, a file, or a database row, in which case the value crosses a boundary that no code path describes. This is the structural reason cross-component findings are usually worse than within-component ones, and it is worth stating as a property of the tool rather than as a defect: the result is a set of components that are individually analysed and a set of interfaces between them that are not. The mitigation is not a better rule but a different discipline: write the interface contract down, state what may cross it and in what shape, and check the pairs that actually exist against each other, which is a small finite task that a human does better than a rule and that no amount of analyser configuration replaces. The first distractor claims the languages are incompatible in principle. The second claims the failure is a configuration gap. questions.explanation: It removes the ability to know the address in advance. A corrupted pointer is only useful if the party who corrupted it can say where it points, and in the ordinary case the address is not something the attacker computed but something the system happened to choose: where the program was loaded, where the library with the function they want was mapped, where the stack sits. If those are the same on every run, a single value is a reliable instrument across every host of that kind, which is what makes an attack reusable and what makes it testable in a laboratory. Randomising the layout each run means the value that worked yesterday is unlikely to work today, so the attacker either has to leak the layout first or has to try a large number of values, and both cost far more than the corruption itself. That is the whole of the contribution, and it is important to be clear that it is a probabilistic defence with two preconditions that are easy to lose. It needs enough entropy that the space is not searchable, and it needs the specific target the attacker wants to be inside the randomised region, since a target in a fixed, known location gains nothing. So randomised layout is a strong measure that is easy to configure into uselessness, and the way to tell whether it is working is to look at whether the addresses a given process uses differ between runs, not at whether the setting is present.

questions.explanation: The difference is in what the attacker has to corrupt and in what survives the corruption. A value in the ordinary stack sits in the same writable memory the attacker is already writing to, and the attack that produced the corruption is generally an unbounded write, so a value that is only four or eight bytes away is simply overwritten along with everything else; the check then fires, but the damage is done and the process is already in a state where continuing is unsafe. Worse, a party that has learned the value by any means can overwrite it with the same value and the check passes, at which point the value protects nothing. A separate stack for return addresses, not writable through the ordinary path, is not reachable by the write that caused the corruption, so the check compares an untouched copy against the frame and finds a real discrepancy; and a party who has not read the stack has no value to restore. The measure therefore defends against the whole unbounded-write family rather than only against the tidy case where the write stopped just short, and it does so by removing the target from the region the attacker is writing to rather than by watching that region. What it does not do is stop the corruption, protect data, or help against a return address that the attacker never corrupted because they found a different way to control the flow. The first distractor describes the canary's weakness, which is the reason the separate stack exists. The second is the reverse confusion, treating a separate stack as a larger version of a value check. The third claims it addresses a different attack entirely.

The service still has to do its job, and a flaw in it is still a flaw in it, and nothing about the account changes what an attacker has to find. What changes is the authority the flaw hands over. An account with no administrative rights cannot install anything, cannot read the credential store, cannot read another user's files, cannot open a listening port, and in most systems cannot see the processes it does not own, so a program that has been made to do something the author did not intend is confined to doing that and to whatever its own identity already allows. questions.explanation: The timing tells the observer how far the comparison got, and how far it got is the position of the first byte that differed. A value that matches for four bytes before failing takes measurably longer to reject than one that fails on the first byte, because all the work up to that point was done, and the difference is small but it is systematic rather than random, so averaging over many attempts exposes it. An observer who repeats the attempt with values that share longer and longer prefixes learns where the secret stops matching them, and can work out the secret one byte at a time from that. The number of attempts this needs is on the order of the length of the secret times the number of possible values per position, rather than the number of possible secrets, which is the difference between a search that is impossible and one that is arithmetic. This is why the comparison is the interesting part rather than the cipher: a well-chosen cipher is not the weak link in a scheme whose value check leaks through how long it takes to reject. It is also worth noticing that the leak is in the rejection path, so it is available to anyone who can cause a comparison and observe the outcome's timing, which in a network service is usually anybody who can send a request. The first distractor describes the length of the input being leaked, which is a different property of a different construction. The second claims the secret is exposed outright, which overstates a statistical signal. The third is the ordinary belief the mechanism defeats, and the reason fixed-time comparison exists at all.

questions.explanation: The rewrite closes the leak only if nothing downstream reintroduces the same dependence. The early return is the obvious source, and removing it is the easy half, but there are two others that survive it. The first is memory access pattern: a comparison that touches its inputs in a data-dependent order, or that indexes into a table in a data-dependent way, leaks through cache and page behaviour even though the instruction count is constant, so a fixed-time comparison has to be both branch-free in the data and regular in the access pattern. The second is the compiler: an implementation that looks branch-free can be transformed back into a branch, and what the source says is not what the built program does, so the only reliable assurance is to inspect the built program or to use a construction whose property the compiler is not free to change. questions.explanation: A deny list is a statement about a set of known things, and the weakness is that the set is bounded by what has been thought of while the interface it constrains is not. Any interface that changes the program counter, that changes the permissions the program holds, or that hands it a way to influence its own execution is a potential route, and a policy that names a few instructions has to enumerate all of them. New instructions are added over time, existing instructions gain addressing modes that did not exist before, and the boundary between one instruction's use and another's is a matter of argument rather than of specification, so the list is always a little out of date. The file's name and its pointer to where the data lives are removed from the directory structure, and the space is marked available for reuse, and the data itself is left where it was until something else is written over it. A running machine is changing its own state continuously: connections and sessions live only in memory, decrypted content exists in memory and not on disk, and anything the machine has not yet written is present only there. Interacting with a running machine to collect from disk also creates changes, because starting tools, opening drives, and running anything on the host writes to it. So a collection that starts with the disk may destroy the memory evidence even while gathering the disk evidence perfectly, and the loss is not recoverable afterwards. questions.explanation: Almost nothing can be concluded about when the activity happened, and that is the useful thing to take from it. The three times are recorded at different points in the file's life and each answers a different narrow question: when the entry was created, when the contents last changed, and when the contents were last read. They are therefore not three measurements of one event, and it is entirely normal for them to disagree. A file copied from another system arrives with the source's times and a new creation time, a file that was edited without the time being updated carries a modification time earlier than the content suggests, and a read that does not update the access time leaves all three stale. What the rule cannot see is the component that the real deployment routes the value through, and that component rejects anything not on a fixed list before the value reaches the sink, so the path the rule found is not the path the value takes. questions.explanation: The fix requires making every observable effect of the comparison independent of the values compared, and the phrase does more work than it appears because there are several observable effects. The early return is the obvious one. The access pattern is the second, since a comparison whose memory behaviour depends on the values is a comparison that leaks through the cache whatever the instruction count does. The third is the built program rather than the source, because a compiler is free to turn branch-free code back into a branch, so the assurance has to come from examining the artefact or from a construction whose property the compiler cannot discard. What is left after the fix is the residual exposure, which is small and real: the fix removes a large statistical signal, not all of it, and a determined party with many samples and a quiet measurement environment can still find something. That is why the mitigation set is a set, and why scheduling controls and the placement of the comparison in the request path are part of the answer rather than an afterthought. Anything the list does not mention is now refused, so a path the program did not take, an interface nobody anticipated, and a change in the processor all produce a refusal and a record rather than an escape. questions.explanation: It changes what a compromised signer can reach, and that is a narrower benefit than it first appears but a real one. With a single vendor key, obtaining it lets a party produce an image that every device in the fleet will accept, so the compromise is total and immediate across the estate. With a per-device key, obtaining one key produces an image that exactly one device will accept, and the estate's exposure is bounded at one device rather than at all of them, and the question of which device was compromised becomes answerable rather than unanswerable. It also means the vendor cannot revoke a single image for the whole fleet without a mechanism to do that, and that mechanism is a revocation list that the devices consult, so the design trades an unbounded compromise for a distribution problem. What it makes harder is everything on the operational side, and it is worth being plain about this because it is why vendors do not do it by default. An image now has to be built and signed once per device, so a fleet of any size needs a build pipeline that can sign at scale and a device count that makes the storage requirements real. An update that has to be recalled has to reach every device. And a device whose key is lost cannot be updated by the same route, so a recovery path has to exist that is not the update route, which is a decision about what a key compromise means. The first distractor understates the benefit. The second is the operational cost, stated correctly. The third is the design decision this trades against.

questions.explanation: The order is set by the fact that the existing fleet has no way to receive the new kind of image, and that has to change before the change can be used or tested. Getting the signing key into devices that do not already have one comes first, and it comes first through a route that does not depend on signed images, because a signed update cannot bootstrap a fleet that cannot verify signatures. Placing the key has to be pinned to a specific authority rather than to a shared store, because a device that accepts any key it holds cannot enforce which kind of image is being authorised, and that decision is the one that cannot be changed later without replacing every device. Only then can a signed image be built, and the first thing to do with it is to verify it on devices that are not in production, since the failure modes are the ones a test fleet exists to find. Deploying to a subset comes next, with the observation window long enough to include the conditions under which the earlier firmware behaved differently, and the general release follows that. The order that publishes the image first is the order in which a fleet receives something it cannot check, and the outcome of a compromise during the rollout would be indistinguishable from a compromise of the vendor's own signing infrastructure.

answer.exemplar: The distinction is between removing a path and removing a precondition, and it is easy to lose because the two produce the same thing at the moment they are checked. A repair changes the program so that the input which caused the fault no longer leads to the fault, and after it the defect is gone: no input produces it, whatever else is true about the environment. A mitigation changes the environment so that the same input no longer leads to the fault, and the defect is exactly where it was, reachable in principle and reachable in practice the moment the precondition stops holding. So the mitigation rests on a claim about how the path works, and that claim is a hypothesis about an implementation rather than a statement about the interface, which is why it is the kind of thing that can be true on the version it was tested against and false on the next one. A team that has a register full of open defects and a programme full of mitigations has a register that is not going to shrink, and the reason is not that the mitigations were badly chosen. It is that the mitigations have done their job, which is to reduce how much the open defects matter, and an open defect whose urgency has been reduced is an open defect that stops being scheduled. The fix for that is not to stop buying mitigations, because for a large class of defects in old code they are the only realistic response and the cost curve is much better than the alternative. The fix is to keep the schedule deliberately rather than letting it follow the feeling of urgency, so the register distinguishes the defects that are being repaired from the ones that are being contained, and the contained ones are still counted as open. There is a second reason the distinction is worth stating, which is that the two are honest in different ways. A mitigation's cost is a permanent operating cost on every machine, paid for by somebody who is not the person who made the decision, and it is usually a setting that can be turned off by a well-meaning person solving a build problem, so a mitigation-based estate quietly degrades and nobody is watching the number. A repair costs development time once and then nothing to operate. So the right answer is a portfolio, chosen per defect, and the thing to avoid is choosing on the basis of which is cheaper this quarter without saying which of the two things has been bought.

questions.explanation: Because the two change different things. Repairing a defect removes a path; a mitigation removes a condition that the path depended on, and the path is still there. The distinction matters because a mitigation has a premise, and the premise is a claim about how the path works, so the mitigation is correct only while the claim holds. When an attacker stops needing the thing the mitigation removed, the mitigation is not weakened, it is irrelevant, and there is usually nothing in the programme that would notice, because the programme's metric measures the presence of the mitigation rather than the presence of the path. It is also worth being clear that mitigations are not the inferior option. They are the only thing available in the window between a defect being understood and it being fixed, they raise the cost of an attack across a whole class rather than one instance, they cost nothing in the developer's time, and for a class of defect that nobody is going to fix they are the whole answer. The mistake is not choosing them and it is not refusing them; it is spending on them while the register still describes the underlying defect as open and nobody is assigned to it. A workable split is that mitigations reduce urgency and a defect with reduced urgency stops being scheduled, so the schedule has to be maintained deliberately. The register is where that has to be visible, and the honest summary of a mitigation-based quarter is that the estate is harder to attack and no less defective.

answer.exemplar: The defensible report says three things: how much of the target the campaign reached, what shapes the corpus contained, and that the result is a statement about the inputs generated rather than about the target. The reason the second of those is the one people leave out is that the corpus is the part of the setup a reader cannot see from the coverage figure, and it is the part that determines what the coverage figure means. A campaign whose corpus contains one well-formed document has explored the neighbourhood of one document, and a defect that needs a document with a particular structure is outside that neighbourhood by construction rather than by bad luck. The coverage number will look respectable, because a parser that accepts a document does reach most of its statement-level code on the first one, and that is precisely what makes the misreport so easy to make. The common wrong report is not a lie, it is a category error: a run with no findings is treated as a finding, and the target is recorded as having been tested rather than as having been partly explored. Once that substitution is made it propagates, because the entry is now evidence that the target is sound, so nobody goes back to it when a defect is later found by hand, and the register records a test that was never as informative as it appears. There is a second failure mode in the other direction which is worth naming because it looks like diligence. A team that keeps a clean run as proof of quality begins to raise the budget, and the budget is often raised past the point where the campaign is finding anything new, so the same entry now supports an inference that the target is difficult rather than that the campaign is finished. The honest practice is to treat coverage as a budget to be managed rather than a score to be maximised, to record the point at which new coverage stopped arriving, and to keep a fixed set of tests for the cases the campaign is structurally bad at. None of this makes fuzzing less valuable; it makes the result mean what it actually says.

The common wrong report calls the target clean.

answer.exemplar: The reason they are complements rather than alternatives is that they act on different preconditions of the same technique, and a technique with two preconditions is removed by taking either one away. The technique in question is reuse of code the program already contains. Its first precondition is that the attacker has code to point at, and when that code has to be written by the attacker it has to live somewhere the program can execute it, which is what the non-executable marking on data pages denies. The second precondition is that the attacker knows where that code is, and code reuse needs no injected instructions at all, so the marking does nothing for it; what the technique needs is an address, and the address is chosen by the system rather than by the attacker, which is what randomised layout denies. So each measure removes one of the two things the technique requires, which is why a programme with both is materially stronger than a programme with one, and why the two are always deployed as a set. The second thing worth saying is that neither of them is a repair, and the way that shows up in practice is that both can be present in a configuration and ineffective. Randomised layout is easy to leave configured in a form that varies over a range far too small to matter, or to switch off entirely when a build that assumed fixed addresses fails, and nothing in the estate then reports a change. Non-executable marking is easy to leave off for a component that needs to generate and execute its own code, and the exception is usually recorded as a note rather than as a finding. That is why the useful question about either measure is not whether the setting is on but whether the property is real in the built artefact: check that the addresses a given process uses differ between runs, and check that the thing an attacker would want to find is inside the region that varies. The third point is about how the two interact with the rest of the estate, and it is the one that decides whether a hardening programme is worth continuing. Each measure raises the cost of one route, and each is probabilistic rather than absolute, so the honest summary is that an attack has to get lucky, and a lucky attack is still an attack. What a programme is actually buying is not the removal of a class but a distribution: many routes, each expensive, so that no single one is worth the effort, and that only works if the measures are independent of each other and each is genuinely in place.

questions.explanation: They close different halves of the same technique. Non-executable data pages remove the route that needs injected instructions; randomised layout removes the prior knowledge that the route which reuses existing code depends on. Either alone leaves a technique open.

answer.exemplar: A digest is a statement about a particular sequence of bytes fed into a particular function. The statement is only as good as the moment it was made, and the moment matters because of what the acquisition process is doing. Copying a device is a sequence of reads and writes that can fail, that is performed by software with its own state, and that is followed by a transfer and an examination during which the copy is opened, mounted, read, and moved between locations. Every one of those is an opportunity for the bytes to change and every one is unobserved. A digest taken at the end of that sequence covers the last part of it, so the property the examiner can state is that the file they hashed is the file they analysed, which is a real and necessary property, and the property they cannot state is that the file they analysed is the device they seized. The break in the chain is exactly at the point where the copy ends and the hashing begins, and the size of the gap is the size of that unobserved interval, which in the scenario described is a week of opening and moving files. This is why the procedure is not a formality and why the timing is specified as being during the acquisition: a digest of the source as it streams past, recorded as the values are produced, ties the copy to the device at the moment of reading, and because reading does not modify the source, the two statements together are what allow a later examination to be placed in the same material as the seizure. The practical consequence is a rule about where the tool runs and what order it does things in, and it is worth noting that this is a tooling question as much as a discipline question, because a tool that streams and hashes in one pass removes the opportunity to get it wrong. There is a related point that people often get wrong in the other direction, which is that a good digest does not date anything. An image of a device that was altered before it was seized is a perfectly consistent image of the device as it was at the moment of seizure, and no amount of hashing will distinguish that from an untouched one; what establishes when a change happened is other evidence, and the register of the case should say so rather than implying that the hash did.

The number should also be read against what the tool is doing, since executions a second is a measure of the harness rather than of the target, and a harness that spends its time in setup rather than in the target is spending the budget somewhere the campaign does not benefit from.

The multi-pass approach exists for a reason that is now historical: on storage that cannot overwrite in place, a single pass can leave the previous contents physically present, so a second and third pass were believed to defeat that.
